#1302. 4 Man Utd Signings Michael Carrick Recommended This Summer

The news is now official: Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager. USMNT manager Mauricio Pochettino is set to replace the Englishman, with GIVEMESPORT sources previously revealing that an agreement in principle over personal terms has been reached.

It will come as no surprise to football fans that Carrick has lost his job. The now-fired coach endured a terrible start to the season, and departs with Man Utd languishing inside the relegation zone, with one win from their opening 10 Premier League games.

Amid the poor results, friction around the club has been apparent, with senior star Lisandro Martinez questioning the summer recruitment at Old Trafford in an explosive interview. It's now emerged that Carrick recommended four signings in the summer transfer window, but the board failed to land any of them.

Carrick's four wanted men are all of high quality and surely would have helped keep him in the job at Man Utd for longer than the 10 league games he managed. Journalist Henry Winter revealed the four footballers, writing on X:

"Sir Jim Ratcliffe will one day have to explain why Manchester United didn’t follow Michael Carrick’s recommendation of the four players he felt the club needed in the summer window – Elliot Anderson, Lewis Hall, Morgan Rogers and, fourth on the list, Mateus Fernandes. Were debt repayments restricting their buying power? Was it simply because United felt the fees were too much for them?"

Mauricio Pochettino has been told by Paul Scholes that he must forget Manchester United pair who will sabotage him.

Anderson was snapped up by Manchester City, with the Etihad side paying £116m to land the English midfielder. Rogers joined Chelsea for £1m more, setting a new record as the most expensive British signing of all time.

Maybe it would be harsh to suggest Man Utd failed massively in not being willing or able to pay such high sums for those two, but it's a sign of the times that the Red Devils were so easily beaten to the star duo by their Premier League rivals.

And there are fewer excuses for Fernandes. While the Portuguese midfileder left West Ham for Tottenham Hotspur, Man Utd were understood to be in the race. No deal was done, though, as Carrick watched another target move to a different club, this time for £85m – with Spurs showing far more ambition in the summer transfer window.

As for Hall, he didn't even move. Instead, Newcastle United convinced him that his immediate future is better served at St James' Park, with the defender signing a contract in September. The Red Devils have needed a left-back replacement for the ageing Luke Shaw, and Hall looks to be the perfect fit. However, as with the three aforementioned, Carrick was once again let down by the club hierarchy.

#1301. Unai Emery's grand plans for Aston Villa after agreeing new contract: Why he believes he can win Champions League, the Pep Guardiola blueprint and changing his mind on selling stars

Published: 07:00 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 07:54 EST, 12 November 2026

Aston Villa hope Unai Emery will become their answer to Sir Alex Ferguson but when planning the current stage of his career the Spaniard had another boss in mind.

Having agreed a new contract that will make him one of the two best paid managers in the Premier League, Emery has the sort of structure at Villa that Pep Guardiola enjoyed for a decade at Manchester City.

Emery has always regarded Guardiola as the world’s best coach – and not just for the teams he has produced and the trophies he has won. The Basque admired Guardiola’s refusal to compromise on his vision for a club and has adopted those principles every step of the way at Villa, leading them from the bottom half to the Champions League.

‘We were speaking about how we can set our project stronger with a (new) deal, yes,’ Emery said last Friday, of a meeting he had with key figures at Villa including co-owner Nassef Sawiris a few days earlier. ‘Nassef is very ambitious, a hard worker and his commitment to the club is huge. It’s easy for me to have meetings with him as normally we are on the same page.’

This season began slowly but after six league games unbeaten, Villa are back in the top half and three points off the top five, as well as sitting sixth in the Champions League group phase with three wins from four.

After Emery underlined his desire to stay at Villa Park, Daily Mail Sport looks at what comes next for him and Villa.

Aston Villa hope Unai Emery will become their answer to Sir Alex Ferguson as he prepares to extend his stay in the Midlands

After a slow start this season, Villa are in fine form in both the Premier League and Champions League

With about two-and-a-half years still remaining on Emery’s previous deal, there was no need for Sawiris to rush. His decision is both a show of faith and a recognition of the current climate.

Emery was on a five-man shortlist to replace Michael Carrick at Manchester United but Daily Mail Sport understands he is unlikely to have moved to Old Trafford even without the contract discussions.

Studying Guardiola convinced Emery that to be successful, a manager needs control. He cannot operate if he has only limited influence over recruitment, or if he has no say in senior appointments – something United are highly unlikely to have granted.

Unlike at many clubs, where sporting directors and heads of performance are brought in by the chairman or chief executive, Emery has driven the key hires at Villa. Since Emery’s arrival, the number of Spanish backroom staff at Villa has grown well into double figures.

Director of football operations Damian Vidagany moved to Villa with Emery in 2022 and was a key reason why Emery accepted the job. Emery also pushed for Monchi to be brought in as ‘president of football operations’ and when that went wrong, he was allowed to select the next guy – Roberto Olabe. It is hard to imagine many other clubs where that would happen.

So far Olabe has been much better than his predecessor, whose dire record in the market saw him ditched a little more than a year ago.

Emery would have had none of this influence at United. In Sawiris, he has a highly supportive boss – contrast that with Sir Jim Ratcliffe. He makes the final calls on recruitment, rather than relying on the equivalent of Jason Wilcox.

Emery’s sense of self-worth is too great and his record too impressive to accept answering to executives of inferior ability. At Villa, he answers only to the ownership group, and he has forged a rock-solid relationship with Sawiris.

Emery was the driving force behind the appointments of director of football operations Damian Vidagany (left) and president of football operations Roberto Olabe (right)

Emery has a rock-solid relationship with co-owner Nassef Sawiris

There are few top clubs these days where the manager has a direct line to the owner but the Sawiris-Emery connection took shape in the autumn of 2022, weeks before he was hired. Sawiris could see the Steven Gerrard experiment was failing and wanted a top-class manager. He looked at Mauricio Pochettino, Thomas Tuchel and Emery.

After a difficult experience at Arsenal, Emery had won the Europa League with Villarreal and was assured by Sawiris that he would have the run of Villa. Emery felt he had never had this level of influence during his 18 months at Arsenal and throughout the process, Sawiris has been as good as his word.

Emery joined on just under £10million per year and his new salary would be close to double that. His wishes in the market have been backed, even when it has been tricky to make the sums add up. Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio were signed on loan at huge expense in January 2025 to deliver Champions League football. That did not happen, but there was no blowback for Emery because Sawiris trusted the direction of travel.

Every one of his requests has been approved. The current stadium redevelopment was planned for 2024 but was shelved because Emery did not wish to play Champions League games in a three-sided ground. Now, he has accepted the bigger picture.

At the training ground, a 40-room hotel was signed off on Emery’s say-so. When Harvey Elliott was brought in on loan and then left in the cold, or when £26m signing Evann Guessand proved a mistake, it was Monchi who took the rap, not Emery.

That sort of loyalty cuts both ways. With their stock so high, how many managers would have stuck around after six of their first-choice starting XI from a Europa League final win had been sold? Emery is taking a risk to his reputation by leading this rebuild but he trusts both himself and Sawiris to get it right.

Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio were signed on loan at huge expense in 2025 to deliver Champions League football. There was no blowback for Emery when that did not happen

When Harvey Elliott was brought in on loan and then left in the cold, or when £26m signing Evann Guessand proved a mistake, it was Monchi (pictured) who took the rap, not Emery

There was a moment at the end of Friday’s press conference when Emery showed just how much he was invested in Aston Villa.

The Spaniard had just been asked if he could elevate Villa to the same level as Europe’s giants and instead of delivering the usual platitudes, Emery referred to the Deloitte Money League, which ranks clubs by the revenue they generate.

To emphasise his point, Emery grabbed his phone, found the page and confirmed that Villa had risen to 14th in the 2024-25 list, generating £376m in that period.

How many top-flight managers are even aware of the Deloitte Money League, let alone their club’s position in it? When asked about finances, most bosses will – quite legitimately – answer that these matters are for senior executives to handle.

Not Emery, who has made a definite shift in recent seasons. He now understands that because of Villa’s financial needs, part of his job will be to sign promising players, increase their value and then – potentially – sell them for double the fee.

This summer, Villa sold Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Ollie Watkins for a combined £253m. They were signed for a total of just £48m.

You can already picture Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi, two of the summer additions, falling into this category.

The unknown is how Emery might feel about this strategy in two or three years’ time if Villa slip out of contention for the Champions League.

Because for all the justifiable enthusiasm about a new contract, this will not be an easy road. Not surprisingly for an overhauled team, Villa are inconsistent.

Villa bought Morgan Rogers (fourth left), Ollie Watkins (fourth right), Ezri Konsa (right) and Youri Tielemans (not pictured) for a combined £48m, then sold them all this summer for £253m

You can already see Johan Manzambi - signed for £52m this summer - being the next player Villa make a huge profit from

After the Europa League triumph in May, Emery's dream is to win the Champions League and last week he made a strong case for saying he could do so with Villa

Throw in their issues with financial regulations and the stadium rebuild and it would be no shock – nor any disgrace – if they finished outside the top five for the next couple of seasons.

Would that be enough for Emery, though? His dream is to win the Champions League and last week he made a strong case for saying he could do so with Villa.

Emery cited Leicester winning the Premier League and his own journey with Villarreal to the Champions League semi-finals in 2022.

Yet the rules are stacked in favour of the wealthiest and no matter how hard they try, Villa may never crack the code. By investing so heavily in Emery, though, Sawiris believes he is giving them a proper shot.

#1300. Italy vs. France: Kick-off time, probable line-ups, team news, where to watch on TV

Get the latest team news ahead of tonight’s Nations League fixture between Italy and France at San Siro, with Sandro Tonali and Francesco Pio Esposito expected to start.

It kicks off at 20:45 CET [19:45 GMT] at the Stadio Meazza in San Siro, Milan.

It’s a match between the top two teams in the Nations League Group A1. France lead the group with ten points, while the Azzurri follow in second with seven.

Only the top two have a guaranteed spot in the Nations League quarter-finals. The final group-stage game will be played on Sunday, with Italy travelling to Belgium.

Italy coach Roberto Mancini will confirm a 4-3-3 system, with Davide Frattesi, Sandro Tonali and Nicolò Barella expected to start in central midfield, and the Esposito brothers, Francesco Pio and Sebastiano, getting the nod up front alongside Nicolò Cambiaghi.

Italian sources this morning confirm that Sebastiano Esposito is the favourite to start on the right wing, with Antonio Vergara as the other option. On the opposite side of the field, Cambiaghi is favourite over Luca Koleosho.

Alphadjo Cisse, Mattia Liberali, Honest Ahanor, Matteo Palma, Federico Gatti and Nicolò Pisilli are the players Mancini sent to the stands for tonight’s fixture.

Kylian Mbappé is not available for France. The Real Madrid star already missed the reverse fixture in Paris on October 2.

The match is available via Amazon Prime Video’s pay-per-view service in the UK and Ireland and Fubo TV in the USA. Football Italia will be among the accredited media at San Siro, providing live updates via a live blog.

Italy (4-3-3): Donnarumma; Kayode, Scalvini, Bastoni, Calafiori; Frattesi, Tonali, Barella; S Esposito, Pio Esposito, Cambiaghi.

France (4-3-3): Maignan; Gusto, Konaté, Upamecano, Truffert; Cherki, Da Cunha, Rabiot; Olise, Barcola, Doué.

#1299. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

There is already a lot of noise from the 2,000 or so Viking FK supporters in the away end.

Last week the club marked their return to the Champions League by securing a famous 3-3 draw with heavyweights Bayern Munich. Viking had led 2-0 at half-time before rescuing a point in the last minute.

A first win of the campaign tonight would represent another huge shock.

Villa’s co-owner Nassef Sawiris is in the house tonight.

Sawiris was the main driver behind the appointment of Unai Emery almost four years ago. Worked out ok, hasn’t it?

Elsewhere in Europe this evening, Manchester United are currently 4-0 down against Cesc Fabregas’ Como. Nico Paz has starred with two goals and an assist. Could this spell the end of Michael Carrick’s tenure in charge of Man Utd? You can keep up with the action and post-match reaction here.

Speaking to the club’s official website in his match preview, the Aston Villa boss said: “Champions League, every team they are playing Champions League, they are because they deserve it and they are dangerous and they have their collective and individual issues or characteristics as a team.

“Viking, they drew against Bayern Munich last week, they lost against Stuttgart. They are with Bodø/Glimt in the league, first and second with the same points.

“Bodø/Glimt is a team successful the last years in Europe, performing well, getting good results, playing Champions League, beating important teams.

“So Viking now is a new team as well, with the with the capacity to draw against Bayern Munich, the capacity as well to compete against Stuttgart and to compete against us tomorrow.

“This is Champions League, and Champions League is very difficult. In Champions League, we have now six points, it’s something amazing, but very difficult, and to keep the same way we are is our challenge.

“It’s not only Champions League, because Europa League is very difficult, and Conference League is very difficult. Europe is always very difficult.

“This is the first respect. We are Champions League, and each team is, of course, very, very respectful for us.”

Ibrahim Mbaye has slowly been embedded into the first team picture at Aston Villa by Unai Emery following his big money to England in the summer. The 18-year-old was used off the bench against Newcastle and looked very likely with his blistering pace and trickery. Mbaye starts this evening and we will be keeping eye on him, given his star quality and talent.

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Aston Villa fairytale under Unai Emery was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, Villa were stepping into the unknown despite the arrival of ten new players.

We have all learned, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their Champions League campaign so far and are running into fine form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

This could be another magical season under their brilliant Basque manager, with an exciting and vibrant new team.

Unai Emery has made four changes to the side that beat Newcastle. From back to front, Pau Torres replaces the injured Wan-Bissaka. In midfield, John McGinn and Ross Barkley come in for Boubacar Kamara and Johan Manzambi. The interesting switch sees Ibrahim Mbaye also start, with Matty Cash the final player to drop out, making the identity of Emery’s last defender a mystery.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Champions League fixture as Aston Villa host Viking in the Midlands.

Villa made history in their previous home Champions League outing last week, thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 to seal the club’s biggest-ever European win. This emphatic victory, coupled with the hard-fought 3-2 triumph over Club Brugge at the start of September, means that Unai Emery’s side have made a 100% winning start to the league phase. The well-deserved 1-0 Premier League victory over Newcastle United at St James’ Park on Saturday evening has amplified the positivity, with Emery’s new-look squad beginning to meaningfully gel and now boast a five-match unbeaten streak across all competitions.

Prepared for another night on Europe's biggest stage ✨ https://t.co/oZYiIiGvRg

Despite their Viking’s lack of European pedigree, Villa should be wary of their Norwegian opponents, who secured an unforgettable 3-3 draw with Bayern Munich in Stavanger last time out in the Champions League. The hosts initially flew into a two-goal lead at the break, before a double from Harry Kane and a strike from Luiz Diaz hauled the Bavarians ahead. However, after Michael Olise was sent off, Herman Haugen’s 90th-minute headed equaliser rescued a thrilling draw to give Viking their European point this season following a 3-1 loss to Stuttgart on MD1. Domestically, the reigning champions of Norway are joint top of the Eliteserien with Bodo/Glimt and embroiled in a nailbiting title race with just seven games remaining.

Villa’s injury list includes Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Johan Manzambi, who both picked up issues against Newcastle, as well as Amadou Onana and Matteo Ruggeri. Still, the hosts possess more than enough quality to dismantle Viking, particularly with Nicolas Jackson, who has been in effective form recently and netted a brilliant brace against Fenerbahce.

We’ll bring you the latest updates and drama. Kick-off is at 20:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1298. Fabrizio Romano Makes Man Utd January Transfer Guarantee as Pochettino Deal Agreed

Manchester United are set to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as their next manager after sacking Michael Carrick.

The Red Devils have had a poor campaign so far and sit in the relegation zone in the Premier League following their worst ever start to a season, with Carrick having led the team to just one win in their opening ten games.

54-year-old Pochettino has been identified as the man to take over, with Man Utd agreeing terms with him to become their next manager, and talks almost finalised with US Soccer to trigger the $12m (£9m) release clauses to bring him and his staff to Old Trafford.

Pochettino's first game in charge will come against Liverpool at Anfield on 22nd November, just days after he is expected to lead the USMNT in their double-header against Haiti before departing, and he will have limited time to work with his new squad before having to select his team.

However, the Argentine will have around six weeks to work with the players and figure out who fits into his plans and what areas of the squad need strengthening ahead of the January transfer window.

United are expected to be in the market for a left-back and a forward at the very least following their shortcomings in the summer transfer window, and Fabrizio Romano has now revealed in his latest YouTube video that Pochettino is set to be heavily involved in the recruitmen during the winter window.

"But then in the first meetings they will have with the club, they will discuss, and that's something they already mentioned in the first contacts had between Pochettino and United," he said.

"They already said very soon we will have specific meetings regarding the January transfer window. Pochettino is a manager who loves to be involved in the transfer strategy. He's not the kind of manager who says, 'Okay, give me the players, I will take care of them.'

"Pochettino is very good also at taking care of what he has. We have to be honest; he's a coach that, especially Tottenham, showed that he can do very good things with players that are not constantly changing. But at the same time, Pochettino likes to be involved. Pochettino likes to have his say, and in this case, I expect Pochettino to be involved at Man United because they need to change.

"Already in January, they need to do something. Could be two, could be three, could be one. I don't know. We will see. But United will sign players in January. I can guarantee that because that's part of the strategy at the club, regardless of who's going to be the coach."

While new arrivals have been 'guaranteed' by Romano during the winter window, United must also start to think about making decisions on the futures of players who are already in the squad.

Harry Maguire, Luke Shaw, Lisandro Martinez, and Bruno Fernandes are all out of contract at the end of the season, with the left-back the only one who doesn't have a club option in his deal for an extra 12 months. But the chances of them all staying beyond this campaign are slim to none, and if Pochettino isn't keen on any of them, then January could be a good chance to move them on and bring in some funds.

Squad planning is an essential part of the success at football clubs, and INEOS have failed miserably so far since taking over footballing control. Pochettino's arrival, and his inclusion in talks about recruitment, are potentially a chance to get back on track, but they must be ruthless as soon as possible.

Mauricio Pochettino has been told by Paul Scholes that he must forget Manchester United pair who will sabotage him.

#1297. Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5. We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells)6. Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 (Rgs2), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

Functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8. Single-cell technologies have revealed extensive new patterns of heterogeneity of specific cell types within the same tissue9, yet their biological importance remains largely undetermined.

Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2. Its specialized metabolism and precise responses to environmental and physiological stimuli make it an ideal model for studying functional cellular heterogeneity. Thermogenic capacity declines substantially with age in rodents and humans, leading to age-related cold sensitivity and metabolic disorders3,4,5, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

BAs and beige adipocytes mediate UCP1-dependent non-shivering thermogenesis10. Although substantial progress has been made in identifying the key pathways that activate thermogenesis, most studies have been conducted at the whole-tissue level, leaving the mechanisms governing its activation, maintenance and deactivation incompletely understood.

The heterogeneity of BAs within the same brown adipose tissue (BAT) and beige adipocyte cluster within inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) has been characterized by our group6 and others5,11,12,13,14. We found that BAs heterogeneously express UCP1 and classified those with low expression as BA-L cells and those with high expression as BA-H cells6. At room temperature, BA-H cells constitute 30–50% of all BAs; BA-H cells predominate after cold exposure, whereas BA-L cells predominate under thermoneutral conditions6. This raises questions of why BA heterogeneity exists, and whether it reflects random variation along a thermogenic continuum or spatially organized, tightly regulated states within the tissue.

Here we identify dynamic bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity controlled by the spatial proximity of BAs to IL-1β puncta through a neuronal–immune regulatory mechanism. This regulation becomes dysfunctional during ageing, leading to cold intolerance in older adults. These findings highlight how different cell types collectively control cellular heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner, integrating environmental and internal cues to regulate tissue metabolism and function.

Reanalysis of our previous single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset6 revealed enrichment of glucocorticoid signalling and GR-target genes in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Top BA-L-cell-enriched genes include H6pd, Rgs2 and thioredoxin-interacting protein (Txnip), whereas BA-H cells were enriched for thermogenesis-related genes, including Ucp1 and cytochrome c oxidase 6B1 (Cox6b1) (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,d–f). Nr3c1 was similarly expressed in BA-H and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f).

We generated Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice for inducible labelling of Ucp1+ cells by crossing the Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Rosa-stop-mT/mG mouse lines (Extended Data Fig. 2a). After 1 week of feeding on a doxycycline diet at room temperature (24 °C), GFP+ and GFP− BAs showed a patchy distribution (Fig. 1a), consistent with BA heterogeneity in AdipoChaser mice6. The Ucp1-rtTA mice used a relatively weak 5 kb Ucp1 promoter15 so GFP is only expressed in UCP1high-expressing BAs (BA-H cells), while Ucp1-cre mice have a strong bacterial artificial chromosome-based Ucp1 promoter that drives Cre expression in all BAs16. Immunofluorescence (IF) staining confirmed selective H6PD expression in BA-L cells (Fig. 1a); 50% of BAs were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD−, 45% were UCP1−(GFP−)H6PD+ and 5% were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD+ (Fig. 1b). Similar heterogeneity was observed in iWAT after 1 week of cold exposure (6 °C) (Fig. 1c), with 45% of these beige adipocytes being UCP1+H6PD−, 49% UCP1−H6PD+ and 6% UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1d). Human BAT showed a similar reciprocal UCP1 and H6PD pattern in multilocular brown–beige adipocytes (Fig. 1e), 45% of BAs were UCP1+H6PD−, 47% were UCP1−H6PD+ and 8% were UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1f). Western blotting confirmed more than twofold higher H6PD in BA-L cells than in BA-H cells and more than fourfold higher UCP1 in BA-H cells than in BA-L cells, while H6PD was enriched in mature BAs relative to in the stromal vascular fractions (SVFs) (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Together, these data identify H6PD as a BA-L marker.

a,b, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice (aged 10 weeks) were fed a doxycycline chow diet for 1 week at 24 °C. Representative images of BAT IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue) (a), and quantification of the relative percentage of BAs positive for GFP+(UCP1+) only, H6PD+ only or both (b). n = 6 per group. c,d, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice aged 10 weeks were fed a doxycycline chow diet for 3 days or 1 week at 6 °C. c, Representative images of IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red) and DAPI (blue) in iWAT. d, Quantification of the relative percentage of BAs positive for GFP+(UCP1+) only, H6PD+ only or both. n = 4 per group. e, Representative IF staining for UCP1 (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue) in human supraclavicular BAT. f, Quantification of the relative percentage of BAs that are positive for UCP1+ only, H6PD+ only or both. n = 5 per group. g, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs from WT mice were reverse-transfected with H6pd Dicer-substrate small interfering RNAs (dsiRNAs) or control dsiRNAs and collected after 2 days. RT–qPCR analysis of H6pd, Rgs2, Hsd11b1 and Ucp1 mRNA levels. n = 3 per group. h–j, 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP mice were injected with lentivirus overexpressing H6PD or mCherry as a control into BAT. h, After 2 weeks, H6PD and β-actin protein levels were analysed using western blotting (WB). i, Representative IF staining of BAT for GFP (green), perilipin (red) and DAPI (blue). j, Quantification of the BA-H cell percentage. For j, n = 5 (mCherry) and n = 4 (H6PD). Statistics were computed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (b, d and f), unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-tests (g (H6pd and Hsd11b1)) or unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (g (Rgs2 and Ucp1) and j); *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001. For b, d, f, g and j, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bars, 25 μm (a (right), c (bottom)), 50 μm (a (left), c (top) and e) and 100 μm (i).

To enable real-time labelling of BA-H cells, we generated Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mice by inserting a P2A-mGFP cassette after Ucp1 exon 6, immediately upstream of the stop codon (Extended Data Fig. 2d). These mice displayed robust BAT GFP fluorescence without altered UCP1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f). GFP IF staining revealed a heterogeneous distribution of GFP+ and GFP− BAs (Extended Data Fig. 2g). In vitro-cultured BAs and beige adipocytes showed selective H6PD expression in GFP− BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 2h), validating our in vivo findings.

We next investigated UCP1-independent thermogenesis through the futile creatine cycle17,18,19,20,21. Tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP) and creatine kinase B (CKB) protein levels increased 4.8-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively, in BAT during cold exposure and were enriched 2.9-fold and 2.0-fold in BA-L cells versus in BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b), consistent with higher Ckb mRNA in BA-L cells6. IF staining further showed TNAP enrichment in BA-L cells (H6PDhigh BAs) in BAT and H6PDhigh beige adipocytes in cold-exposed iWAT (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). In vitro-differentiated BAs also displayed selective TNAP expression in BA-L cells (GFP− BAs) (Extended Data Fig. 3e), indicating that the futile creatine cycle is more active in BA-L cells.

Regarding the metabolic differences between BA-L cells and BA-H cells, BA-L cells have half the basal respiration, but similar maximal respiration compared to BA-H cells, indicating similarly high mitochondrial potential6. Using in vivo [U-13C]glucose tracing22, we recently showed that BAT has the most active glucose oxidation among metabolically active tissues, while in vitro tracing confirmed active glucose oxidation in differentiated BAs23. To characterize BA-L metabolism, we performed [U-13C] glucose and [U-13C] palmitate tracing in freshly isolated BA-H cells and BA-L cells, followed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Fully labelled (m+16) free palmitate (C16:0) was about twofold higher in BA-L cells, indicating greater fatty acid uptake (Extended Data Fig. 4b), while fully labelled total palmitate was sixfold higher, suggesting preferential fatty acids storage in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 4c). BA-L cells also showed lower citrate enrichment from both tracers, indicating lower glucose and fatty acid oxidation (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Thus, BA-L cells exhibit greater fatty acid uptake and accumulation but lower fatty acid and glucose oxidation, consistent with their lower basal respiration6.

We next examined whether H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells. H6PD depletion in BAs differentiated from BAT SVFs of Ucp1-mGFP mice increased Ucp1 expression sixfold (Fig. 1g), indicating that H6PD negatively regulates Ucp1. Conversely, H6pd overexpression by lentiviral injection into BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f) significantly reduced the proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 1i,j). Thus, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L that regulates UCP1 expression and BA heterogeneity.

H6PD localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and generates endoplasmic reticulum-resident NADPH, distinct from cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)24. H6PD primarily determines the reductase activity of endoplasmic reticulum-localized 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD11B1), which converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol25. GR protein levels were similar between BA-H cells and BA-L cells, indicating that GR signalling is not regulated by receptor abundance (Extended Data Fig. 3b). We next investigated whether GR signalling regulates UCP1 expression. Simultaneous treatment of BAs differentiated from the SVFs of wild-type (WT) mice with 11-dehydrocorticosterone (11-DHC), a natural substrate for active glucocorticoid biosynthesis25, and noradrenaline (NA) substantially increased UCP1 protein (Fig. 2a). However, 24 h 11-DHC pretreatment blunted NA-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2b). Thus, prolonged activation of GR signalling suppresses BA responsiveness to NA, maintaining BA-L cells in a stable, low-thermogenic status.

a–c, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs of WT mice were treated with NA ± 11-DHC for 24 h (a) or pretreated with vehicle or 11-DHC for 24 h, followed by NA (b) or forskolin (c) treatment for 24 h. UCP1 and β-actin immunoblots and quantification. n = 3 independent cultures. Co-treat, co-treatment; pretreat, pretreatment. d–f, BAs were pretreated with vehicle or 11-DHC for 48 h, followed by NA (d), forskolin (e) or 8-BrcAMP (f) treatment for 30 min. Immunoblots and quantification of phosphorylated PKA substrates and β-actin are shown. n = 3 independent cultures. g, BAs were pretreated with vehicle or RU-486 for 1 h, followed by NA with or without DEX treatment for 24 h. Immunoblots and quantification of UCP1 and β-actin are shown. n = 4 independent cultures. h, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice (aged 10 weeks) were on a doxycycline chow diet for 1 week at 24 °C. BAT IF staining for GFP (green), RGS2 (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue), and quantification of single- or double-positive BAs are shown. n = 4 per group. i, BAs were treated with vehicle or DEX for 2 h and subjected to ChIP using anti-GR antibody or control IgG. ChIP–qPCR analysis of Rgs2 promoter (−92 bp to +53 bp), presented as the percentage of input DNA. n = 4 per group. j, RT–qPCR analysis of Rgs2 in three-dimensionally cultured primary BAs, treated with vehicle, DEX, CL-316,243 or DEX + CL-316,243 for 24 h. n = 3 per group. k–m, BAs were reverse-transfected with Rgs2 or control dsiRNAs. k, Rgs2 mRNA was analysed 2 days after. Cells were then pretreated with 11-DHC for 24 h and stimulated with NA for 30 min. l,m, Immunoblots (l) and quantification (m) of phosphorylated PKA substrates and β-actin. n = 3 per group (k) and n = 4 per group (m). Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (a–h, j and m), unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-tests (i (GR) and k) and unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (i (IgG)); ***P < 0.001. NS, not significant. For a–g, i–k and m, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bar, 50 μm (h).

Forskolin activates adenylyl cyclase (AC) to generate cAMP26. 11-DHC pretreatment also blocked forskolin-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2c), suggesting inhibition of AC activity or downstream cAMP signalling. To determine where GR signalling acts within the canonical β-adrenergic receptor–cAMP–PKA pathway that controls UCP1 expression27, we measured PKA activity in in vitro-differentiated BAs after 24 h of 11-DHC pretreatment, followed by NA, forskolin or 8-BrcAMP (a cAMP derivative). 11-DHC pretreatment markedly reduced NA- or forskolin-induced PKA activity (Fig. 2d,e), but not the response to 8-BrcAMP (Fig. 2f), indicating that downstream cAMP signalling is not affected by GR activation. Thus, GR signalling potentially suppresses UCP1 expression by inhibiting AC-mediated cAMP production.

Whereas 11-DHC requires conversion to active glucocorticoids, dexamethasone (DEX) directly activates GR. In contrast to the delayed effect of 11-DHC, DEX suppressed NA-induced UCP1 expression after co-treatment (Fig. 2g), an effect that was abrogated by the GR antagonist mifepristone (RU-486) (Fig. 2g). Similarly, in the in vitro-differentiated BAs, CL-316,243 increased Ucp1 expression about 3-fold, whereas DEX pretreatment reduced this induction to about 1.6-fold (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Together, these data support the conclusion that GR activation maintains BA-L cells in a low-UCP1-expressing state by suppressing cAMP production.

We next investigated how GR signalling regulates BA heterogeneity. DEX is commonly used in adipogenic differentiation cocktails; its withdrawal increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.8-fold in BAs differentiated from BAT SVF of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Conversely, 11-DHC and the active glucocorticoid corticosterone decreased the BA-H/BA-L ratio compared with in the DEX-free control, independent of differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In WT mice, DEX induced BAT whitening and reduced the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 74% (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Thus, manipulating GR signalling alters BA heterogeneity both in vitro and in vivo.

To determine how GR signalling inhibits cAMP production, we examined other BA-L-enriched genes. Rgs2 was highly expressed in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f). RGS2 binds to the C1 domain of AC III, V and VI, attenuating Gαs-dependent cAMP accumulation28. IF staining confirmed selective RGS2 expression in BA-L cells, with 40% of BAs being UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2−, 55% UCP1−(GFP−)RGS2+ and 5% UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2+ (Fig. 2h). RGS2 was also selectively expressed in GFP− BA-L cells in in vitro-differentiated BAs (brown and beige) (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). Analysis of published GR chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by sequencing datasets29 identified GR occupancy within the promoter and intronic regions of Rgs2 (Extended Data Fig. 5i). ChIP–quantitative PCR (qPCR) in in vitro-differentiated BAs confirmed GR binding at the Rgs2 promoter, which was enhanced by DEX (Fig. 2i). Lastly, DEX increased Rgs2 mRNA 2.2-fold in freshly isolated BAs (Fig. 2j), supporting Rgs2 as a GR target. Thus, RGS2 is a GR target in the BAs that inhibits cAMP production. Knocking down Rgs2 in in vitro-differentiated BAs (Fig. 2k) did not affect PKA activity in response to NA alone (Extended Data Fig. 5j,k). However, Rgs2 knockdown abrogated the inhibitory effect of 11-DHC pretreatment on NA-induced PKA substrate phosphorylation (Fig. 2l,m). Rgs2 is therefore a GR target in BAs that suppresses Ucp1 expression by inhibiting AC activity, and BA-L cells are stabilized in the low-thermogenic state through the GR–RGS2–AC signalling axis.

H6PD protein levels in BAT changed inversely with UCP1 across environmental temperatures, while GR protein was only slightly elevated at thermoneutrality (30 °C) (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Cold exposure reduced H6PD protein by 1.8-fold in iWAT, but not in gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c), suggesting thermogenic-depot-specific regulation. CL-316,243 similarly decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d). H6pd mRNA decreased rather than increased with rising temperature in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6e), indicating post-transcriptional regulation. Thus, H6PD protein levels, but not mRNA levels, change dynamically in BAT in response to fluctuating environmental temperatures, which may be essential for altering the BA-H/BA-L ratio in response to thermogenic demand.

Sympathetic neurons secrete NA to activate BA thermogenesis. We next tested whether sympathetic innervation mediates cold-induced H6PD protein reduction using unilateral BAT denervation, validated by reduced tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) protein (Fig. 3a). Cold exposure increased BA-H cells from 31.1% to 85.6% (Fig. 3b), as previously reported6. Denervation prevented the cold-induced reduction of H6PD (Fig. 3a), and although there was an increase in the BA-H/BA-L ratio, the proportion of BA-H cells was 66% lower than the sham group during cold exposure (29.1% versus 85.6%) (Fig. 3b). The low BA-H/BA-L ratio was accompanied by BA whitening (Extended Data Fig. 6f), a feature associated with impaired thermogenesis30. Notably, H6PD consistently labelled BA-L cells regardless of the variable BA-H/BA-L ratio at different environmental temperatures (Fig. 3b). Thus, sympathetic innervation is required to reduce H6PD protein and raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio after cold exposure.

Cold exposure also downregulated GR target genes, including Rasd1, Fkbp5, Pik3r1, Tsc22d3 and Rgs2 in BAT, whereas denervation blunted these effects (Extended Data Fig. 6g), supporting the involvement of GR signalling in raising the BA-H/BA-L ratio. We next tested whether the opposite occurred when shifting mice from cold to thermoneutrality. H6PD protein increased 2.1-fold in BAT, while GR protein remained unchanged (Fig. 3c). Transitioning cold-exposed mice to 30 °C also restored GR target gene expression in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6h), indicating that H6PD and GR signalling dynamically respond to temperature fluctuations to regulate BA heterogeneity.

We next tested whether blocking GR during the transition from cold to warmer temperatures prevents BA-H cells from switching to BA-L cells. We generated a BA-H-specific, inducible Nr3c1-knockout model by crossing Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Nr3c1flox/flox mice (Fig. 3d). Mice were first exposed to 6 °C for 1 week to raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio, followed by 1 week of doxycycline diet under cold conditions to induce Nr3c1 deletion in BA-H cells (Ucp1-Nr3c1flox/flox turning into Ucp1-Nr3c1−/−), and were then returned to room temperature with the doxycycline diet for another week. One week is long enough for the mice to reduce thermogenesis according to the rise in environmental temperature. IF staining confirmed Nr3c1 deletion in most BAs (Fig. 3e), consistent with 86% of BAs being BA-H cells during cold exposure (Fig. 3b), and western blotting showed reduced GR and RGS2 in isolated BAs (Fig. 3f). We previously showed that BA-H cells contain smaller lipid droplets and therefore have higher density, whereas BA-L cells have larger lipid droplets, lower density and float after mild centrifugation (like white adipocytes)6. Notably, BAT from Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice sank in PBS, whereas control BAT floated (Fig. 3g), suggesting a higher density and a higher BA-H/BA-L ratio. Consistently, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed browner BAT with smaller lipid droplets, increased iWAT beiging (Fig. 3h) and a higher proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 3i). Metabolic cage studies further showed increased energy expenditure and oxygen consumption in Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice, without changes in body weight (Fig. 3j,k and Extended Data Fig. 6i), body composition, food intake, respiratory exchange ratio or locomotor activity (Extended Data Fig. 6j–n). As the controls were metabolically healthy young adults, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed no further improvements in glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). These data highlight stage- and cell-subtype-specific requirements for GR signalling to regulate bistable BA states and thermogenesis. Inhibition of GR reactivation during the transition from cold to room temperature preserved a high BA-H/BA-L ratio and persistent thermogenesis despite reduced environmental thermogenic demand. These data not only confirm that we can block the BA-H-to-BA-L switch by inhibiting GR signalling, but also indicate that manipulating BA heterogeneity can increase thermogenesis and significantly boost whole-body energy expenditure.

To elucidate the sympathetic regulation of H6PD protein, we treated in vitro-differentiated BAs with NA but observed no change in H6PD protein (Fig. 4a), suggesting that other cell types and factors are involved in sympathetic regulation of H6PD. We next assessed cytokine expression in BAT and found that Il1b exhibited the greatest reduction (by 53%) after cold exposure (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7a), and the greatest induction (by 3.3-fold) when mice were shifted from cold to thermoneutrality (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7b). Cold-induced Il1b suppression was blunted by BAT sympathetic denervation (Fig. 4b), while NA reduced Il1b expression in BAT explants (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Il1b was predominantly expressed in SVFs rather than in mature adipocytes (Fig. 4d) and its expression changed with environmental temperature (Fig. 4d). qPCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) analysis further confirmed the predominant expression of Il1b in CD45+ SVFs (Fig. 4e), indicating an immune cell source. By contrast, systemic IL-1β levels remained unchanged across environmental temperatures, suggesting local regulation of IL-1β levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 7d).

Notably, IF staining revealed that BA-L cells clustered around IL-1β puncta, whereas BA-H cells formed clusters further away (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 7e), a pattern that was observed across room temperature, during cold exposure and after denervation (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Quantification indicated that IL-1β puncta and GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) show a significant negative Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC = −0.5 ± 0.1), suggesting a mutually exclusive pattern between these two factors at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 7f). During cold exposure, this pattern persisted but was weaker (PCC = −0.2 ± 0.1), as fewer IL-1β puncta were available for quantification (Extended Data Fig. 7f). BAT denervation prevented the reduction in IL-1β puncta, maintained a low BA-H/BA-L ratio and preserved a strong negative correlation with GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) (PCC = −0.45 ± 0.1). Thus, across all three conditions, BA-L cells were consistently close to IL-1β puncta, indicating a strong correlation between IL-1β and BA heterogeneity.

We next tested whether IL-1β regulates H6PD protein levels in BAs. Among the proinflammatory cytokines tested, TNF and IL-1β increased H6PD protein levels by 1.8- and 3.5-fold, respectively (Fig. 4g), without increasing H6pd mRNA (Extended Data Fig. 7g), confirming a post-transcriptional regulation of H6PD. Combined IL-1β, TNF and IFNγ treatment did not further increase H6PD protein beyond the effect of IL-1β alone (Fig. 4g). IL-1β increased H6PD protein in a time-dependent manner (Fig. 4h). During cycloheximide (CHX) treatment, H6PD abundance decreased by 30% and 50% at 6 and 12 h, respectively, whereas IL-1β prevented this decline (Fig. 4i), indicating increased H6PD protein stability from degradation. IL-1β is known to activate multiple downstream pathways, including JNK, MEK–ERK, p38–MAPK and IKK–NF-κB. Among inhibitors targeting these pathways, only the MEK and ERK inhibitor U0126 attenuated IL-1β-induced H6PD upregulation (Extended Data Fig. 7h,i), indicating that MEK–ERK mediates IL-1β-induced H6PD stability.

We next examined whether IL-1β regulates UCP1 expression. IL-1β did not alter UCP1 expression in the in vitro-differentiated BAs in the absence of 11-DHC, but reduced UCP1 protein levels by 53% in the presence of 11-DHC (Extended Data Fig. 7j,k), indicating that IL-1β suppresses UCP1 through GR signalling.

Adipose-tissue-resident immune cells can regulate sympathetic innervation31,32,33. However, TH and synaptophysin staining showed similar sympathetic innervation of BA-H cells and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 7l,m), indicating that IL-1β regulates BA heterogeneity independently of differential sympathetic innervation.

To identify the immune cells that secrete IL-1β in BAT, we integrated multiple published BAT scRNA-seq datasets14,34,35,36,37 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). β-Adrenergic receptors were expressed in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), suggesting potential sympathetic regulation. Subclustering analysis revealed that Il1b was enriched in neutrophils (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−CXCR2+), monocytes (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−Ly6C+), and macrophages (CD45+CD11b+F4/80+) (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). Flow cytometry confirmed that IL-1β was mainly produced by CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a,b), with IL-1β+ cells predominantly comprising neutrophils and macrophages, but not monocytes (Extended Data Fig. 9c–e). IL-1β+ cells represented 10% of neutrophils and 1% of macrophages, indicating that IL-1β production is restricted to specific subsets (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Despite the low frequency, the greater abundance of macrophages resulted in substantial numbers of IL-1β+ macrophages, with IL-1β+ neutrophils only 1.7-fold more abundant (Extended Data Fig. 9e), indicating that both cell types are major IL-1β sources. IF staining further confirmed IL-1β colocalization with subsets of CXCR2+ neutrophils and F4/80+ macrophages in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 9f,g).

Depletion of CD45+ immune cells from BAT SVFs increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.7-fold without affecting overall differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j), supporting a role for immune cells in regulating BA heterogeneity. To further confirm the role of local IL-1β in thermogenic regulation, we injected lentivirus encoding Il1rn (encoding IL-1RA), a naturally occurring inhibitor of IL-1 receptor signalling, or an mCherry control directly into BAT (Extended Data Fig. 10a). IL-1RA increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio twofold in mice housed at room temperature (Fig. 4j,k). In in vitro-differentiated BAs, Il1r knockdown attenuated IL-1β-mediated suppression of UCP1 expression, indicating a direct effect of IL-1β on BAs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Moreover, in vivo pharmacological inhibition of IL-1β production using the caspase-1 inhibitor VX-765 increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.2-fold (Extended Data Fig. 10c,d), further demonstrating a functional role for IL-1β in regulating BA heterogeneity.

We next investigated how temperature fluctuations regulate IL-1β in BAT. Il1b expression in primary BAT SVFs was temperature-dependent (Fig. 4d), whereas IL-1β+ immune cell numbers remained unchanged across housing temperatures (Extended Data Fig. 10e–h), indicating regulation independent of immune cell recruitment. NA directly suppressed Il1b expression in BAT-derived CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 10i), suggesting adrenergic regulation of IL-1β production. Consistent with adrenergic receptor expression in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), scRNA-seq analysis showed selective expression of Adrb1 and Adrb2, but not α-adrenergic receptor genes, in Il1b-expressing immune cell populations (Extended Data Fig. 11a). We further examined adrenergic regulation of Il1b using bone marrow-derived neutrophils. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced Il1b expression dose dependently (Extended Data Fig. 11b), whereas NA pretreatment suppressed this induction in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). This effect was reversed by the non-selective β-adrenergic receptor antagonist propranolol, but not by the non-selective α-adrenergic receptor antagonist phenoxybenzamine (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Consistently, propranolol administration, but not phenoxybenzamine, increased Il1b expression in BAT in vivo (Extended Data Fig. 11g,h), supporting β-adrenergic suppression of IL-1β production.

Decreased BA thermogenesis has been reported with obesity38 and ageing3. However, high fat diet- (HFD)-induced obese mice were completely cold-tolerant, with 100% survival after 7 days of cold exposure (Fig. 5a,b). HFD feeding decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels (Fig. 5c), indicating preserved BAT thermogenic potential. By contrast, aged mice exhibited cold intolerance, with reduced body temperature and a 25% mortality within the first 2 days (Fig. 5d,e), suggesting impaired thermogenesis. Aged mice showed a 2.3-fold increase in H6PD and a 40% decrease in UCP1 (Fig. 5f), suggesting a reduced BA-H/BA-L ratio. GR was modestly reduced by HFD feeding but unchanged with ageing. These differences suggest that cold-induced thermogenesis is more severely impaired with ageing than with obesity at a young age, and that the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying impaired thermogenesis may differ substantially.
